reading.body:
Lenovo's US arm filed 10 Lobbying Disclosure Act reports naming AI, and those filings name 16 separate bills.

The filings are spread across eight lobbyists, but two of them carry most of the load. Jon Beamer appears on all 10, Heather Smith on 9. The remaining six names appear on five or fewer, and two of those, Andrew Ginsburg and Yelena Vaynberg, appear on two each. That concentration matters because lobbying disclosure records the filer and the issue, not the argument. A firm that files for a client reports that it lobbied on an issue, not the position it argued. So the count of filings tells you how persistently Lenovo's Washington operation touched AI, not what it asked for.

The bill list is the more useful signal. Sixteen distinct bills named in filings dated 2025 or later is a wide net for a single client, and it is the pattern you would expect from a hardware company whose products sit under AI export controls, procurement rules, and chip supply restrictions. Compute is the constraint on AI scaling, and compute is a physical supply chain that runs through trade law. A company that sells the machines AI runs on has reason to be in front of a large number of bills at once.

What this data does not cover is the substance. It does not say which bills Lenovo supported or opposed, what any lobbyist argued, or how much was spent. It does not connect these filings to data center construction, power procurement, or grid interconnection, because the filings do not name those subjects. The reader should treat this as a map of attention, not of influence.
